PHASE 4 · ADVANCED PRIMARY CARE CLINICAL MANAGEMENT

Week 73 — Lesson 97: COPD Management

FNP-level goal: Confirm and stage the COPD care problem, reduce symptoms and exacerbation risk, optimize inhaler and nonpharmacologic support, assess acute deterioration safely, and coordinate long-term follow-up.

Learning Objectives

  • Distinguish suspected COPD from asthma, heart failure, infection, PE, malignancy, and other dyspnea causes.
  • Assess symptom burden, exacerbation history, smoking/vaping, spirometry context, inhaler use, comorbidity, and function.
  • Use current guideline-informed inhaler strategy, technique review, prevention, and rehabilitation support.
  • Recognize exacerbation, hypoxemia, hypercapnia, pneumonia, and respiratory-failure red flags.
  • Build a feasible action plan, tobacco-treatment plan, and referral/follow-up pathway.

Part 1 — Confirm the Disease and the Current Problem

COPD is a chronic airflow-limitation syndrome usually associated with exposure history and persistent respiratory symptoms, but chronic cough and dyspnea have many causes. Confirm objective testing and clinical context when stable, and reconsider diagnosis when onset, variability, imaging, response, or systemic features are atypical. Asthma-COPD overlap, heart failure, PE, anemia, infection, medication effects, malignancy, and anxiety may coexist.

Part 2 — Symptoms, Exacerbations, and Function

Ask about dyspnea, cough/sputum change, wheeze, exercise tolerance, sleep, weight, fatigue, hospitalization, prior ventilation, systemic steroid/antibiotic exposure, urgent visits, oxygen use, inhaler technique, tobacco/vaping, occupational exposure, and social support. Exacerbation history predicts future risk. Functional decline may be as important as spirometry: can the patient walk, bathe, shop, eat, and manage medicines safely?

Part 3 — Stable COPD Care

Inhaler selection follows current evidence, symptoms, exacerbation history, comorbidity, technique, device ability, cost, and adverse-effect risk. Before changing therapy, confirm diagnosis, adherence, device technique, refill access, and trigger/exposure reduction. Smoking cessation is the highest-impact intervention for many patients and should be approached with evidence-informed treatment plus respectful repeated support, not blame.

Vaccination, pulmonary rehabilitation, activity/conditioning, nutrition, inhaler education, infection prevention, comorbidity management, and advance-care planning when appropriate all belong in longitudinal care. Oxygen requires appropriate clinical assessment and safety education; do not assume it is indicated merely because a patient is short of breath.

Part 4 — Exacerbation and Emergency Triage

Assess change from baseline, work of breathing, respiratory rate, oxygenation when available, mental status, ability to speak, chest pain, fever, sputum change, edema, volume status, reliever response, and concern for alternative emergencies. Severe distress, cyanosis, altered mental status, exhaustion, rising oxygen need, inability to maintain oxygenation, silent/markedly diminished breath sounds, hypotension, or suspected PE/ACS/sepsis requires emergency evaluation.

Part 5 — Action Plan and Follow-Up

Give a plain-language plan for baseline care, early worsening, emergency warning signs, inhaler use, smoking cessation support, and follow-up after an exacerbation. Own pending imaging/lab/referral results. Consider pulmonary referral for uncertain diagnosis, frequent exacerbations, advanced symptoms, difficult inhaler strategy, possible oxygen/ventilation assessment, or concern for another diagnosis.

Clinical Case

A 67-year-old with COPD has increased dyspnea, purulent sputum, reduced appetite, and confusion. Family reports a new oxygen requirement.

FNP reasoning: this is not a routine refill visit. Assess immediate respiratory and hemodynamic risk; consider COPD exacerbation plus pneumonia, hypercapnia, sepsis, heart failure, PE, or ACS. Confusion and new oxygen need lower the threshold for emergency evaluation.

FNP COPD Framework

  1. Confirm/reconsider diagnosis using symptoms, exposures, testing, and mimics.
  2. Assess control and risk: symptoms, function, exacerbations, hospitalizations, and oxygen needs.
  3. Optimize treatment: current guideline strategy, technique, adherence, access, smoking cessation, and rehabilitation.
  4. Triage change from baseline: work of breathing, oxygenation, mentation, infection/cardiac/PE concerns.
  5. Close loops: action plan, follow-up, referrals, preventive care, and escalation precautions.

High-Yield Summary

COPD care: combines confirmation, symptom/function assessment, exacerbation prevention, inhaler technique, and tobacco treatment.
Before escalation: check diagnosis, device technique, adherence, access, and mimics.
Emergency signs: severe distress, confusion, cyanosis, exhaustion, hypotension, new oxygen need, or concern for another acute disease.
FNP standard: treat the person’s baseline, trajectory, function, access, and safety—not dyspnea in isolation.

Clinical safety note: This lesson is educational. COPD diagnosis, spirometry, inhaler strategy, oxygen, exacerbation treatment, referral, and emergency disposition must follow current guidelines, policy, scope, and the individual patient’s presentation.
